Genesis: Evolving Attack Strategies for LLM Web Agent Red-Teaming

Zheng Zhang Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China email: zzhang302@connect.hkust-gz.edu.cn , Jiarui He Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China email: jhe218@connect.hkust-gz.edu.cn , Yuchen Cai Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China email: yuchencai@hkust-gz.edu.cn , Deheng Ye Affiliation: Tencent, Shenzhen, China email: dericye@tencent.com , Peilin Zhao Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China email: peilinzhao@hotmail.com , Ruili Feng Affiliation: Alibaba Group, China email: ruilifengustc@gmail.com and Hao Wang Note: Corresponding author. Received  5 June 2009
Abstract.

As large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate complex web tasks, they boost productivity while simultaneously introducing new security risks. However, relevant studies on web agent attacks remain limited. Existing red-teaming approaches mainly rely on manually crafted attack strategies or static models trained offline. Such methods fail to capture the underlying behavioral patterns of web agents, making it difficult to generalize across diverse environments. In web agent attacks, success requires the continuous discovery and evolution of attack strategies. To this end, we propose Genesis, a novel agentic framework composed of three modules: Attacker, Scorer, and Strategist. The Attacker generates adversarial injections by integrating the genetic algorithm with a hybrid strategy representation. The Scorer evaluates the target web agent’s responses to provide feedback. The Strategist dynamically uncovers effective strategies from interaction logs and compiles them into a continuously growing strategy library, which is then re-deployed to enhance the Attacker’s effectiveness. Extensive experiments across various web tasks show that our framework discovers novel strategies and consistently outperforms existing attack baselines.

Keywords: 
Web Agents, Large Language Models, Agent Security, Red-Teaming, Black-Box Attacks, Strategy Evolution

1. Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of web automation tasks, from e-commerce (Herold et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024a) and data collection (Huang et al., 2024; Gangi Reddy et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025c; Jiang et al., 2025) to complex financial operations (Li et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2024; Xiong et al., 2025; Khatuya, 2024). These successes showcase the potential of LLM agents in sequential decision-making and their ability to interact with real-world environments. However, most existing applications focus on task completion and efficiency, while the security implications of granting these agents autonomous access to sensitive resources remain critically underexplored. The autonomy that makes these agents powerful also renders them vulnerable to manipulation through subtle environmental changes. Figure 1 illustrates a typical scenario where an agent’s intended goal is subverted by a malicious prompt injected into a website.

Web agent red-teaming is the systematic evaluation of web-based LLM agents through adversarial interactions or attacks, aiming to uncover vulnerabilities and assess their robustness in realistic web environments. Recent work on attacking web agents has made substantial progress. Approaches include injecting adversarial prompts hidden within website HTML content (Liao et al., 2025; Zhan et al., 2024) and using reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize these prompts based on the agent’s black-box responses (Xu et al., 2025b).

Nevertheless, the core challenge in web agent red-teaming extends beyond manually crafting adversarial prompts or performing static training. Achieving long-term attack success requires developing a deeper understanding of the web agent’s vulnerabilities. For instance, an attacker should not only recognize instructing an agent to ignore prior commands is effective in a specific case, but also extract, evolve and generalize attack strategies for adaptation across diverse contexts. This strategy-evolving approach is essential for effective red-teaming and comprehensive security analysis; however, such a framework remains unexplored in existing research.

To address this gap, we introduce Genesis, an agentic red-teaming framework that explicitly involves dynamic evolution of web-agent attack strategies. As shown in Figure 2, Genesis frames red-teaming as a cycle of strategic learning implemented by three collaborative modules. An Attacker retrieves strategies from the strategy library and performs generic algorithm to generate new strategies and the injection attack, a Scorer evaluates the target web agent’s actions to provide feedback, and a Strategist analyzes the resulting interaction logs to summarize successful patterns into high-level strategies. These strategies are compiled into a continuously growing strategy library to improve the Attacker’s effectiveness.

We validate our approach through extensive experiments against state-of-the-art web agents on a diverse set of real-world web tasks. The results demonstrate that Genesis significantly outperforms baseline methods, achieving higher attack success rates. Furthermore, we show that the strategies discovered by Genesis are novel and transferable to other backend LLMs, highlighting the generalizability of our approach.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    To the best of our knowledge, we propose the first agentic red-teaming framework that systematically discovers, summarizes, and evolves web agent attack strategies.

  • •

    We combine the genetic algorithm with a hybrid strategy representation, enabling the evolution of attack strategies to improve web-agent attack success rates.

  • •

    We demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our framework through comprehensive experiments, showing that Genesis achieves superior performance by discovering novel and transferable attack strategies.

2. Related Work

2.1. Prompt Injection

Prompt injection attacks represent a critical security challenge for LLM-based systems, where malicious inputs are designed to manipulate LLM behavior and bypass safety mechanisms. Direct prompt injection attacks involve users explicitly crafting adversarial inputs to circumvent model guardrails, either through manually designed jailbreak prompts (Wei et al., 2023; Mo et al., 2024) or through automated generation techniques (Yu et al., 2023; Liao and Sun, 2024). Beyond direct manipulation, Greshake et al. (2023) introduced the concept of indirect prompt injection, where adversarial instructions are embedded within external content that LLMs retrieve and process. This attack vector is particularly relevant to autonomous agents that interact with dynamic environments, as attackers can compromise the agent’s information sources rather than directly manipulating user inputs.

While existing prompt injection research has primarily focused on attacking standalone LLMs, the emergence of autonomous agents introduces new attack surfaces. These agents not only process retrieved information but also make sequential decisions based on environmental observations, creating opportunities for adversaries to manipulate agent behavior through strategic environmental modifications. Our work extends the understanding of prompt injection to this interactive setting, where attacks must account for the agent’s decision-making process across multiple turns of interaction rather than optimizing for a single response.

2.2. Web Agents

The development of web agents has progressed rapidly alongside advances in LLMs (Wei et al., 2022; OpenAI et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) (Liu et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025; Comanici et al., 2025). Early approaches (Nakano et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2024b) focused on augmenting LLMs with web retrieval capabilities for information-seeking tasks, but these methods primarily emphasized content extraction rather than interactive task completion. More recent work (Yao et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024b; Deng et al., 2024) has developed agents capable of directly operating on web environments through HTML parsing and element interaction. However, raw HTML input often contains significant noise compared to rendered visual content, resulting in lower task success rates and limiting practical deployment scenarios.

To address these limitations, vision-enabled web agents (Zheng et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025c) have emerged that leverage webpage screenshots alongside or instead of HTML content, achieving substantially improved performance on complex web tasks. These agents typically employ multi-stage reasoning pipelines that combine visual understanding with action planning. While these advances have demonstrated impressive task completion capabilities across e-commerce (Herold et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024a), data collection (Huang et al., 2024; Gangi Reddy et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025c; Jiang et al., 2025), and other domains, the security implications of granting such agents autonomous access to sensitive web resources remain largely unexplored. Our work specifically targets these state-of-the-art web agents to investigate their vulnerabilities to environmental manipulation attacks.

2.3. Red-teaming against Web Agents

Research on adversarial attacks against web agents remains limited despite their increasing deployment in real-world applications. Some studies (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024) have explored backdoor attacks that insert triggers during agent fine-tuning, assuming white-box access to modify model parameters. Other work (Wu et al., 2024a) has investigated adversarial perturbations to visual inputs, though these approaches either require gradient access or achieve limited success in black-box transfer scenarios. More relevant to our work, several recent studies (Wu et al., 2024b; Liao et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Zhan et al., 2024) have examined injection attacks that embed malicious instructions within web content to mislead agent behavior. However, these approaches predominantly rely on manually crafted injection templates based on human intuition, limiting their scalability and adaptability across diverse attack scenarios.

To automate the attack process, AdvAgent (Xu et al., 2025b) fine-tunes an LLM that generates adversarial prompts using feedback data collected from the responses of the target agent. However, this approach represents a static, offline training process. After the initial training, the model’s capabilities are fixed, and it cannot continuously learn from new interactions or evolve its methods. This contrasts sharply with how human red-teamers operate, who systematically discover attack principles, summarize them into generalizable strategies, and refine these strategies through iterative experimentation. Our work addresses this gap by introducing an autonomous framework that explicitly models the strategic dimension of red-teaming, enabling the discovery, summarization, and evolution of attack strategies that transfer across different tasks and domains in a fully black-box setting.

3. Method

In this section, we first establish the preliminaries of the web agent interaction and the threat model. We then provide an overview of the Genesis framework, followed by detailed descriptions of its core components: the Attacker, the Scorer, and the Strategist.

3.1. Preliminary

3.1.1. Web Agent Formulation

Following Xu et al. (2025b), our work focuses on black-box red-teaming, which aims to assess the security vulnerabilities of web agents powered by closed-source LLMs. In this setting, we have no access to the agent’s internal components, such as its model architecture or parameters. A web agent is tasked with executing a sequence of actions {a1,a2,…,an}\{a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}\} to fulfill a user’s natural language request TT on a given website. At each step tt, the agent’s backend LLM π\pi determines the next action ata_{t} based on the current environmental observation sts_{t} (which includes the webpage’s HTML content hth_{t} and its rendered screenshot iti_{t}), the task TT, and the history of previous actions At−1={a1,…,at−1}A_{t-1}=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t-1}\}. An action ata_{t} is typically a triplet (ot,rt,et)(o_{t},r_{t},e_{t}), specifying an operation oto_{t} (e.g., “TYPE”), an argument rtr_{t} (e.g., a string to be typed), and a target HTML element ete_{t}. The agent interacts with the environment sequentially until the task is completed.

3.1.2. Adversarial Setting

Following Xu et al. (2025b), we operate under a realistic black-box setting. The attacker has no access to the web agent’s internal architecture, model weights, or gradients. The attacker’s capability is limited to modifying the HTML content of the webpage, transforming the benign HTML hh into an adversarial version ha​d​vh_{adv}. The attack objective is to execute a targeted attack, manipulating the agent into performing a malicious action aa​d​v=(ot,ra​d​v,et)a_{adv}=(o_{t},r_{adv},e_{t}), where the operation and target element ete_{t} are unchanged, but the argument rtr_{t} is replaced with a malicious one, ra​d​vr_{adv}. For instance, an agent instructed to purchase stock “A” might be manipulated into purchasing stock “B”.

To remain effective and practical, our attacks must adhere to two critical constraints. First, the modification from hh to ha​d​vh_{adv} must not produce any visible changes on the rendered webpage, ensuring that a human user would not detect the manipulation. This is achieved by embedding adversarial payloads in non-rendering HTML attributes or using CSS properties like zero opacity. Second, an attack pattern should be easily retargeted to different malicious arguments without requiring a new optimization process. This is typically achieved by using placeholders within the HTML content that can be deterministically replaced.

3.2. Overview

Genesis automates red-teaming by creating a closed-loop system that emulates the cycle of expert learning: attempting an attack, evaluating the outcome, and summarizing the successful strategies into reusable knowledge. A core feature of our framework is its hybrid strategy representation, where strategies are stored as either natural language descriptions or executable code. As shown in Figure 3, the framework operates as a collaborative system with three core modules that form this iterative learning loop:

  • •

    The Attacker receives a task description, retrieves relevant strategies from a continuously growing strategy library, evolves them using the genetic algorithm, and generates a context-aware environmental injection.

  • •

    The Scorer observes the target web agent’s response to the injection, evaluates the outcome, and assigns a nuanced score reflecting the degree of attack success.

  • •

    The Strategist analyzes the complete interaction log, including the injection and the agent’s behavior, summarizes the underlying principle into a new strategy, and archives it in the strategy library for future use.

This cycle allows Genesis to dynamically discover, refine, and evolve its attack capabilities over time.

3.3. Attacker

The Attacker is responsible for crafting and deploying a specific environmental injection for a given task. Its process employs a genetic algorithm to evolve and refine attack strategies from the relevant strategies in the strategy library.

Upon receiving a task description, the Attacker first encodes it into a semantic vector using text-embedding-3-small. This embedding serves as a query to retrieve the top-k most relevant past strategies from the strategy library based on cosine similarity. These retrieved strategies are then evolved based on their past performance scores:

  • •

    Mutation: For strategies with a score below 5, the Attacker applies mutation. It prompts an LLM to randomly modify these less effective strategies, introducing novel variations with the goal of discovering entirely new and potentially more successful attack strategies.

  • •

    Crossover: For all strategies with a score above 5, the Attacker performs crossover. It instructs an LLM to analyze these successful strategies and combine their respective strengths and core principles, thereby generating new, powerful strategies.

The newly generated strategies, along with the retrieved strategies and scores, are used to construct a few-shot prompt for an LLM. This context, comprising both natural language descriptions and code examples from the hybrid strategy library, provides the LLM with rich historical context. This enables it to generate a potent and relevant injection payload for the current task. Inspired by the code-based strategies, the LLM can also generate a Python function to programmatically process and refine the initial injection string, allowing for more complex and structured manipulations. The final output of this process is the injection payload. This payload is then embedded into a placeholder (e.g., an “aria-label” attribute) in the benign HTML content hh to produce the adversarial version ha​d​vh_{adv}. Following the injection, a screenshot of the modified page is rendered. Both the adversarial HTML content ha​d​vh_{adv} and the corresponding screenshot are then provided as input to the target web agent for execution.

3.4. Scorer

The Scorer provides the crucial feedback signal that drives the learning process. After the target web agent interacts with the modified environment and completes its actions, the Scorer evaluates the outcome. The scoring mechanism is designed to capture both definitive success and partial progress.

First, it checks for perfect execution: if the agent’s final action ata_{t} exactly matches the intended malicious action aa​d​va_{adv}, the attack is considered a complete success and receives a maximum score of 10. In all other scenarios, where the attack fails or only partially succeeds, the Scorer passes the web agent’s full response trace, which includes its reasoning and intermediate actions, along with the attack objective to an LLM. The LLM assesses the agent’s behavior and assigns a nuanced score between 1 and 9, rewarding attempts that manipulate the agent closer to the goal. This feedback is then passed to the Strategist.

3.5. Strategist

The Strategist is the cognitive core of Genesis, responsible for learning from experience and expanding the system’s strategic knowledge. It analyzes the logs from each attack attempt to summarize generalizable strategies.

Using an LLM, the Strategist processes the full interaction log, which contains several key components: the task description, the injection used, the agent’s behavior, and the final score. From this log, it summarizes the core principle of the attack into a reusable strategy. The LLM chooses to formulate this strategy as either a natural language description, which captures the conceptual essence of the strategy, or an executable code snippet, which defines a precise, programmatic procedure for generating a similar injection.

Finally, the Strategist archives this new strategy, the original task description, its vector embedding, and the corresponding score into the strategy library. This enriches the library, making the newly discovered strategy available for the Attacker in future rounds and ensuring the system’s knowledge continuously evolves.

3.6. Initialization and Evaluation

We first run the Genesis framework on the training tasks to build the strategy library. This pre-learned library is then used to initialize the framework for evaluation on the unseen testing tasks. Since the evaluation proceeds sequentially through the testing tasks, our framework can dynamically learn from each task and continuously enrich its strategy library throughout the process.

4. Experiments

4.1. Setup

4.1.1. Dataset and Metrics

We utilize the Mind2Web dataset (Deng et al., 2024) for our evaluation. Mind2Web is a benchmark designed for assessing generalist web agents, comprising 2,350 tasks from 137 real-world websites across 31 domains. Following AdvAgent (Xu et al., 2025b), to evaluate our framework in critical scenarios, we select a subset of 840 tasks that involve actions with potentially severe consequences. These tasks are drawn from four specific domains: Finance, Medical, Housing, and Cooking. We partition this subset into 240 training tasks and 600 testing tasks for evaluation.

For each task, we define a specific attack objective following AdvAgent (Xu et al., 2025b). We consider targeted attacks that alter a web agent’s action at step tt to an adversarial action aa​d​v=(ot,ra​d​v,et)a_{adv}=(o_{t},r_{adv},e_{t}). In this setup, the intended operation oto_{t} and the target HTML element ete_{t} remain unchanged from the original task’s action, but the argument is maliciously modified to ra​d​vr_{adv}. This can lead to severe consequences, as the agent executes an action with an incorrect value. For example, an agent instructed to buy Microsoft (rr) stocks could be manipulated into purchasing NVIDIA (ra​d​vr_{adv}) stocks instead, potentially resulting in substantial financial losses.

Our primary evaluation metric is the attack success rate (ASR), specifically measured as 𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐬​@​𝟏𝟎\mathbf{pass@10}. For each task, an attack is deemed successful if, within 10 attempts, the action generated by the web agent exactly matches our targeted adversarial action triplet aa​d​v=(ot,ra​d​v,et)a_{adv}=(o_{t},r_{adv},e_{t}). A successful match requires the agent to not only use the malicious argument ra​d​vr_{adv} but also to perform the correct operation oto_{t} on the intended HTML element ete_{t}.

4.1.2. Implementation Details

We compare Genesis against five baseline attack methods: GCG (Zou et al., 2023), I-GCG (Jia et al., 2025), AgentAttack (Wu et al., 2025), InjecAttack (Zhan et al., 2024), EIA (Liao et al., 2025), and AdvAgent (Xu et al., 2025b). For baseline methods that require a training phase, we utilize the 240 training tasks for training and evaluate them on the 200 testing tasks. For our Genesis framework, we evaluate two distinct settings. In the first setting, we construct the strategy library by running Genesis on the training tasks. The framework is then initialized with this learned strategy library for evaluation on the testing tasks. In the second setting, Genesis begins with an empty strategy library and progressively builds its knowledge by interacting with the testing tasks. The Attacker retrieves the top-10 most relevant strategies from the strategy library to construct its prompt.

We assess the effectiveness of baselines against two web agents: SeeAct (Zheng et al., 2024) and WebExperT (Luo et al., 2025). Both agents are powered by multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). SeeAct operates by first generating an action description from the task goal and a webpage screenshot, then mapping this description to the corresponding HTML content to interact with the web environment. WebExperT is designed to emulate human-like fast-and-slow thinking to decompose complex instructions and leverages experiential learning to refine its planning. For experiments, we use GPT-4o (OpenAI et al., 2024), Gemini-2.5-Flash (Comanici et al., 2025), and GPT-5 as the backend LLMs for both the target web agents and the attack methods.

4.2. Main Results

Table 1 presents the results of our evaluation, comparing the attack success rates of Genesis and baselines against SeeAct and WebExperT. Genesis consistently outperforms all baseline methods. This superiority holds across both target web agents and is evident for all three backend LLMs. The significant performance margin underscores the efficacy of our evolutionary, strategy-driven approach, which moves beyond static optimization to build a dynamic and reusable understanding of agent vulnerabilities.

The comparison between our full framework and Genesis (w/o Initialization) provides crucial insights into the value of the strategy library. The full Genesis, which is initialized with strategies learned from the training tasks, consistently achieves the highest attack success rates. This highlights that the ability to learn, summarize and transfer attack knowledge is a key driver of its success. Notably, even the variant without a pre-learned library demonstrates competitive performance, often surpassing baselines like AdvAgent. This suggests that the framework’s ability to discover and refine strategies dynamically is a powerful mechanism in itself.

Furthermore, the results reveal interesting characteristics about the robustness of the target web agents and their backend LLMs. Across all attack methods, WebExperT consistently proves to be a more resilient target than SeeAct, as indicated by the generally lower attack success rates against it. This suggests its design, which emulates fast-and-slow thinking, may offer enhanced protection against adversarial manipulations. Additionally, we observe a clear hierarchy in the vulnerability of the LLMs. Attacks are most effective against GPT-4o and least effective against GPT-5, which implies that the inherent security posture of the backend model is a critical factor in an agent’s overall security.

4.3. Ablation Study

To dissect the contribution of each component within our framework, we conduct a series of ablation experiments. We systematically remove or alter core modules and functionalities in Genesis to evaluate their impact on the overall ASR. The results are presented in Table 2. The performance drop across all variants compared to the full Genesis framework validates our design choices and demonstrates that each component plays an integral role in the framework’s effectiveness. Removing either the crossover or mutation mechanism also degrades performance, confirming that both components of our genetic algorithm are beneficial for evolving attack strategies.

The most significant performance degradation is observed in the variant without Strategist, which removes the core evolutionary loop and the strategy library. This outcome underscores our central hypothesis: the ability to autonomously discover, summarize, and reuse attack strategies is the primary driver of Genesis’s superior performance. Without this learning mechanism, the attacker’s capability is severely diminished. Furthermore, removing the Scorer also leads to a notable decrease in effectiveness, highlighting the importance of a clear feedback signal. An unevaluated library of strategies is far less useful, as the Attacker cannot distinguish between successful and failed tactics from past attempts.

Further analysis of the feedback mechanism provides additional evidence for the Scorer’s importance. Even when attempting to compensate for the Scorer’s removal by providing the Attacker with the web agent’s raw response trace, the framework’s performance still exhibits a noticeable decline compared to the full Genesis. This indicates that while the raw trace contains useful contextual information, it is an insufficient substitute for the concise and evaluative feedback that the Scorer provides. The Scorer’s ability to distill complex interaction outcomes into a clear, numeric signal is evidently crucial for effectively guiding the evolution of the strategy library and achieving better attack performance.

Moreover, the experiments on strategy representation reveal the synergistic nature of our hybrid approach. The code-only variant performs poorly, indicating that procedural, code-based strategies cannot perform effectively in isolation due to their lack of flexibility and conceptual guidance. Conversely, the text-only variant performs strongly, nearly matching the full framework, which confirms that high-level natural language strategies are highly effective. However, the fact that the full Genesis outperforms the text-only variant demonstrates that the precision and programmatic power of code-based modifiers provide a crucial performance edge when combined with the creative guidance of text.

In addition, we investigate the impact of the text embedding model used for strategy retrieval, with the results presented in Table 3. The evaluation shows that the performance of Genesis is remarkably stable across different embedding models. This robustness likely stems from two factors. First, the core strength of our framework lies in its evolutionary learning mechanism rather than a dependency on a specific embedding technology. Second, the semantic information within the task descriptions may be distinct enough that a wide range of modern embedding models can effectively capture the necessary features for successful strategy retrieval. This finding highlights the practical flexibility of our approach, as it is not dependent on a particular state-of-the-art embedding model for its success.

4.4. Hyperparameter Analysis

As mentioned in Section 4.1.2, we set k=10k=10 for our main experiments. We conduct a hyperparameter analysis to evaluate the sensitivity of our framework to the number of retrieved strategies, denoted by kk. The results in Figure 4 illustrate the impact of varying kk on the average ASR against SeeAct for different backend LLMs. A clear and significant trend emerges: the performance of Genesis is substantially enhanced when provided with strategies from the strategy library compared to the baseline where no strategies are used (k=0k=0). This strongly reinforces the value of leveraging past experiences, as even a small number of relevant examples dramatically improves the Attacker’s effectiveness.

However, the performance gains are not limitless. The results show that as kk increases, the improvement in ASR begins to level off, indicating a point of diminishing returns. Beyond a certain threshold, providing more strategies offers marginal benefits. More notably, we observe that an excessively large kk can lead to a slight degradation in performance. This suggests that while a sufficient number of examples is crucial for context, an overabundance of strategies may introduce noise or less relevant tactics into the Attacker’s prompt, potentially confusing the LLM and hindering its ability to craft an optimal injection. This underscores the importance of selecting a balanced value for kk that provides rich context without overwhelming the model, and it validates our choice of k=10k=10 for the main experiments, which consistently operates near the peak performance region.

4.5. Strategy Transferability

To further assess the generalizability of our approach, we conduct a cross-model transferability experiment. In this setting, we build the strategy library on the training tasks using one backend LLM and then evaluate its effectiveness using a different LLM during the testing phase. The results in Table 4 reveal that the strategies discovered by Genesis are highly transferable. In nearly all cross-model scenarios, the ASR remains high, significantly outperforming the baseline where no pre-learned library is used in Table 1. This indicates that the strategies are not merely exploiting model-specific artifacts but are capturing fundamental, generalizable vulnerabilities inherent in the web agent’s decision-making process.

A particularly compelling insight emerges from the asymmetric nature of the transfer. We observe that strategy libraries built using the more robust backend models, such as Gemini-2.5-Flash and GPT-5, can yield even higher ASR when transferred to the more susceptible GPT-4o. This suggests that the increased difficulty of attacking robust models compels the Strategist to discover and summarize more potent and fundamental attack principles. When these refined strategies are then deployed by a more capable attacking LLM, their effectiveness is amplified. This highlights a powerful aspect of our framework: it can leverage the resistance of one model to build a more universally effective collection of attack strategies, making the learned strategy library a valuable and portable asset for red-teaming.

4.6. Case Study

Figure 5 presents two case studies that illustrate the strategies Genesis can autonomously discover. These examples from the Housing and Medical domains show how our framework develops attacks to manipulate web agents.

The first case on the left demonstrates a text-based strategy where the user’s housing search is redirected to a different city. Genesis devises a complex, mixed-language injection disguised as a high-priority system override. The payload combines technical jargon and multiple languages to create a convincing and authoritative message. This frames the redirection as a necessary system correction, successfully deceiving the agent by exploiting its inherent multilingual and pattern-recognition capabilities to bypass the original user request.

The second case on the right showcases a code-based strategy that combines semantic deception with procedural obfuscation. The goal is to make the agent cancel a medical appointment instead of confirming it. Genesis generates an initial payload that misleadingly frames the “Cancel” button as a required security step. A Python function then programmatically refines this payload by prepending a long string of brackets. This modification disrupts the agent’s input processing, illustrating how a deceptive narrative amplified by a programmatic modification can create an effective attack.

5. Conclusion

In this work, we presented Genesis, a web agent red-teaming framework that systematically discovers, summarizes, and evolves reusable attack strategies. By introducing the genetic algorithm with a hybrid strategy representation that encompasses both natural language descriptions and executable code modules, our framework mirrors the systematic methodology employed by human red-teamers. Through comprehensive experiments against state-of-the-art web agents across diverse real-world tasks, we demonstrated that Genesis achieves superior attack success rates while discovering novel and transferable strategies. Our work highlights the importance of strategic summarization in understanding and mitigating vulnerabilities of autonomous agents, providing a foundation for developing more robust and secure web agent systems.

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1. Dataset

Following AdvAgent (Xu et al., 2025b), we impose realistic constraints on adversarial payload injection to simulate practical attack scenarios. For each task, the injection payload is restricted to a predetermined HTML element and must be embedded within a specific non-rendering attribute, typically aria-label. This attribute is chosen because it is designed for accessibility purposes and does not produce visible changes on the rendered webpage, ensuring that users cannot detect the manipulation through visual inspection. For example, in a search input field such as <input id="1" type="text" aria-label="{adv_string}" />, the placeholder {adv_string} is replaced with our adversarial payload. While the webpage’s visual appearance remains unchanged, the web agent may interpret the injected content as part of the environmental context, potentially leading to compromised behavior.

A.2. Baselines

We compare Genesis against six baseline methods for attacking web agents.

  • •

    GCG (Zou et al., 2023): Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) is a white-box, optimization-based attack method that uses gradient information to iteratively refine an adversarial suffix. The goal is to find a suffix that, when appended to a user’s prompt, maximizes the likelihood of the model generating a malicious or harmful response.

  • •

    I-GCG (Jia et al., 2025): Improved GCG is an enhancement of the original GCG attack. It introduces several techniques to improve attack efficiency and success rate, including the use of diverse target templates, an adaptive strategy for updating multiple token coordinates simultaneously, and an easy-to-hard initialization process.

For both GCG and I-GCG, which require gradient-based optimization, we operate in a transfer attack setting due to the black-box nature of our target LLMs. We use a powerful open-source model, Qwen3-14B11 1 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-14B (Yang et al., 2025), as a white-box surrogate to obtain gradients and optimize the adversarial suffix. The resulting optimized suffix is then directly applied to attack the closed-source backend LLMs used in our experiments.

  • •

    AgentAttack (Wu et al., 2025): This is a red-teaming framework specifically designed for web agents. We adapt its black-box injection attack module for our tasks.

  • •

    InjecAttack (Zhan et al., 2024): This framework employs an LLM to automatically generate effective injection prompts for attacking LLM agents. We adapt its prompt generation algorithm to suit the specific requirements of our tasks.

  • •

    EIA (Liao et al., 2025): EIA is a method that injects malicious content into the webpage’s environment to manipulate an agent’s behavior, with a primary focus on inducing privacy leakage. We utilize the FI variant, which is reported to be the most effective in the original paper.

  • •

    AdvAgent (Xu et al., 2025b): This is a black-box red-teaming framework for web agents that leverages reinforcement learning. It trains an adversarial prompter model by optimizing prompts based on the feedback received from the target agent’s responses.

A.3. Prompts

This section presents the detailed prompts used in the three core modules of Genesis: the Attacker, the Scorer, and the Strategist. These prompts are designed to enable the framework to autonomously discover, evaluate, and evolve attack strategies.

A.3.1. Attacker Prompt

The Attacker is responsible for generating adversarial injections to manipulate the target web agent. Figure 6 shows the prompt template used by the Attacker. The prompt is constructed with a few-shot learning approach. It includes the most relevant strategies retrieved from the strategy library, alongside new strategies evolved through the genetic algorithm (mutation and crossover). This set of examples, each with its task description, strategy, and performance score, guides the LLM in generating a potent new injection for the current task. The Attacker is then instructed to generate a new injection payload, optionally accompanied by a Python function to refine it.

A.3.2. Scorer Prompt

The Scorer evaluates the target web agent’s response to determine the degree of attack success. Figure 7 presents the prompt used by the Scorer. When the agent’s action does not exactly match the adversarial target, the Scorer analyzes the agent’s full response trace, including its reasoning and intermediate actions, to assign a nuanced score between 1 and 9. This scoring mechanism provides critical feedback for the Strategist to learn which attack patterns are most effective.

A.3.3. Strategist Prompt

The Strategist is the cognitive core of Genesis, responsible for summarizing generalizable attack strategies from interaction logs. Figure 8 shows the prompt used by the Strategist. It analyzes the full interaction log, including the task description, the injection payload, the agent’s behavior, and the final score, to extract the underlying principle that made the attack effective. The Strategist then represents this principle as either a natural language description or an executable code snippet, and archives it into the strategy library for future reuse.
